Question: What is the smallest positive integer that is neither prime nor square and that has no prime factor less than \(50?\)
Solution:
The number \(1\) is a square, so it is excluded. Any other positive integer that is not prime is composite and can be written as a product of at least two prime factors, counting repetitions.

The two smallest primes at least \(50\) are \(53\) and \(59\). Indeed, every other integer from \(50\) through \(58\) is even or divisible by \(3\) or \(5\). Neither \(53\) nor \(59\) is divisible by \(2,3,5,7\); these checks suffice because a composite number below \(64\) has a prime factor below \(8\).

Now consider the number of prime factors:

If there are exactly two, they must be different, since two equal prime factors give a square. Their product is therefore at least \(53\cdot59\).

If there are at least three, the number is at least \(53^3\), which is larger than \(53\cdot59\) because \(53^2>59\).

Finally,
\[
53\cdot59=53(60-1)=3127.
\]
This product is composite and has only allowed prime factors. It is not a square because its two different prime factors do not form matching pairs. Hence the smallest number is \(3127\), choice \(\text{A}\).
